note: Local colour for the Draft Table: what locals eat, drink, say, do and tell. `roles`: the kind of neighbourhood it is easiest to find in.

colour.summary: Chunks of eel stewed with parsley and baked under a thick crust, sold hot from the cookshops on fish days.
Wheat boiled in milk with eggs, saffron and currants, eaten at every feast and by the sick the rest of the year.
Whatever is in the pot, every day: beans, leeks, oats and a bit of bacon if the week went well.
Thin spiced wafers with sweet spiced wine, served at the end of a feast to anyone the host wants to impress.
Barrels of salted herring eaten all through Lent, until everybody swears they will never eat another.
Ale brewed by every alewife in town, each sure hers is best, tested by the ale-taster who is never sober.
Honey mead from the abbey bees, strong, sweet and said to make you honest.
Pear cider from the old orchards, drunk at harvest and blamed for everything that happens at harvest.
What townsfolk say when asked what {city} is made of, usually with a shrug and a look at the river.
Said when anything is over and done with, from the bell that tells every household to cover its fire.
A warning to newcomers, which means both the actual town ditch and the people who live beside it.
On Twelfth Night people sing to the apple trees, pour cider on their roots and bang pots to scare off bad spirits.
A bush or pole hung over a door means fresh ale is ready inside, and anyone may come in and buy a jug.
The parish brews a great batch of ale and holds a feast to raise money for the church roof, which always needs mending.
Most houses leave a dish of milk on the step for the good folk, and nobody admits to believing in them.
Locals tell of a church that slid into the water long ago; on still nights you can hear its bells ringing under the waves.
An old oak on the common is said to be where a giant green knight once rode in and challenged the lord's men.
Old folk say a king sleeps under the hill with his knights, to wake when the land needs him most.
People say a witch lives in the forest who will help anyone who asks politely, and curse anyone who doesn't.
Everyone knows the miller keeps a thumb on the scale; the rumour is that he has two, and the second is the reeve's.
The talk in the taverns is that the abbey cellar holds more wine than the whole town drinks in a year.
Rumour says the wizard's tower is full of gold, and every few years someone tries to find the door.
Dark, sticky oatmeal gingerbread with treacle, baked for Bonfire Night and better a week after.
Tripe stewed in milk with onions, the works' favourite supper and a dish no visitor ever asks for twice.
Split peas boiled in a cloth and eaten hot with saveloys, from a shop that always smells of it.
Oysters so cheap the poor eat them by the dozen, from barrows on every corner.
The new working-class supper, fried in dripping and wrapped in yesterday's paper.
Biscuits from a sourdough starter carried west in someone's coat, the town's oldest living thing.
Beef and chiles stewed in an iron pot, sold by the chili queens on the plaza at night.
The ranch cook's stew of everything but the hide, the horns and the holler.
The local brewery's bitter, drunk by the pint and argued about by the gallon.
The temperance drink of the town, sweet and fizzy, ordered loudly by men who want to be seen ordering it.
Saloon whiskey of uncertain making, said to be mostly alcohol, tobacco, pepper and gunpowder.
What the mill owners say about the smoke, and what the workers say back with a different look on their faces.
Said when something is ready to go, from the engine sheds, and now used for everything from babies to dinner.
Frontier talk for still alive and above ground, as in "Not bad, I'm still above snakes."
Before the works hooter, a knocker-up taps on bedroom windows with a long pole to get the shifts out of bed.
Everybody walks the promenade or the park on Sunday afternoon in their best clothes, to see and be seen.
Visitors leave their guns at the marshal's office or the hotel on the way into town, and collect them on the way out.
Young women pack supper boxes that are auctioned to the young men, who then eat with whoever packed theirs.
Old-timers swear a prospector found a vein of pure gold in the hills and died before he could tell anyone where.
The grand hotel is said to be haunted by a lady in grey who waits on the stairs for a husband who never came back.
Night-shift workers swear they have seen an airship with no lights pass silently over the moor.
The gossip is that the mill master's daughter has been seen walking out with a union man.
Everyone has heard which way the new line will run, and everyone has heard it differently, and bought land accordingly.
Thick creamy chowder, argued over endlessly: tomatoes or no tomatoes, and the wrong answer starts fights.
Every diner's meat, potatoes and a vegetable on a blue divided plate, the cheapest square meal in town.
Frankfurters in a bun with mustard, the one thing everyone agrees tastes better at the ballpark.
The new modern dish at every church supper: fruit, vegetables or both, set in shimmering gelatine.
The Italian families' Sunday dinner that the rest of town has started ordering on Wednesdays.
Gin made in somebody's bathtub, flavoured with juniper oil and hope, and mixed with anything to hide the taste.
Milk, seltzer and chocolate syrup, no egg and no cream, from the soda fountain.
The legal half-percent beer, which the bartender will happily 'needle' with alcohol if you know how to ask.
The flappers' word for anything excellent, used until everyone's father starts using it too.
What you say at a speakeasy door, though every door in town has a different Joe.
How everyone in town buys their radio, their car and their furniture, and how they mean to pay for their sins.
Families pile into the new car after church for a slow drive out to the country and back, with a picnic if the tyres hold.
Crowds gather outside the radio store to hear the ballgame on the loudspeaker, cheering at the window.
Every summer family gathering is a clambake on the beach, clams, corn and lobster steamed under seaweed.
The town's minor league ball club, who have not won a pennant since before the war and get cheered anyway.
Fishermen say a rum runner sunk by the Coast Guard still runs his boat on foggy nights, with no lights.
People say there are tunnels under downtown from the old days, now used to move liquor between the hotels.
Everyone has a theory about which bootlegger pays the mayor, and none of them are flattering.
The gossip columns hint that a society heiress is seeing the drummer from the jazz club.
The five-and-dime on Main Street, where every kid in town spends their allowance on Saturday.
Lobster on a buttered split-top bun, hot with butter or cold with mayo, and the town has strong feelings about which.
Egg, cheese and bacon on a roll from the corner deli, the town's real breakfast whatever the cafes say.
The slice place by the college, open till three, where every night out ends.
Warm cider donuts rolled in cinnamon sugar from the orchard stand, the first sign that fall has come.
The taco truck outside the hardware store, which has more loyal customers than any restaurant in town.
The brewery's flagship IPA, on tap in every bar in town and named after a local landmark.
Locals drink iced coffee all year round, even in January, and visitors find this alarming.
What locals tell lost tourists, only half joking, about the roads round {city}.
Used to mean very, as in wicked good or wicked cold, by anyone who grew up here.
The local way to measure time; everyone remembers where they were in the big storm and what it took.
Every church and half the bars do a Friday fish fry, and the queue at the fire hall's goes round the block.
On the first warm day of spring the whole town is out on the patios in shorts, whatever the thermometer says.
In October the town fills with visitors driving slowly to look at the trees, and locals complain about the traffic.
Tuesday trivia at the pub is serious business, with team names that are puns and a rivalry going back years.
The minor league team, with a mascot everyone loves, cheap tickets and fireworks on Friday nights.
Friday night football at the high school, the whole town in the bleachers and the rivalry game in October.
The old family hardware store on Main Street that sells nails by the pound and knows how to fix your problem.

names: The ghost of the old mill
colour.summary: Teenagers dare each other to spend the night in the old mill, where a worker is said to walk at midnight.
Locals tell visitors about the thing in the lake with a straight face, and there is a festival for it in August.
Everyone has heard that a big company is buying up the waterfront, and nobody knows who started the rumour.
Supposedly a famous actor has bought a house out on the point, and someone's cousin saw them at the farmers' market.
The old emergency ration bars, which children are fed once a year so they know what the founders lived on.
Stew of the mushrooms grown in the dark decks, the most common dinner aboard and everyone's mother's recipe.
Green noodles made from spirulina, eaten in broth at every noodle bar and better than they sound.
A real hen's egg, rare and prized, given as a birthday present and eaten with ceremony.
A cake built layer by layer in a food printer, in whatever shape you ask for, for every celebration.
Gin distilled from whatever the farms overproduced, flavoured with herbs from the garden deck, strong and clear.
Black tea grown on the terraces, stewed strong with a lot of sugar, drunk at every shift change.
Said instead of goodbye, a reminder from the old days to check your seals and look after each other.
Everyone's grandmother's motto, from when nothing aboard could be replaced.
What people say before quoting something the founders probably never said, to win an argument.
Anything old-fashioned, impractical or extravagant is 'very Earthside', said fondly or not.
On your birthday you walk the whole length of the ship, bow to stern, and people you pass wish you well.
Every newborn gets a plant in the arboretum named after them, and people visit theirs all their lives.
Families book an hour at the big window once a week to sit together and look at the stars.
Every corridor has a swap shelf where you leave what you don't need and take what you do, no questions.
The rival zero-g ball teams of the decks, whose matches fill the arena and settle nothing.
Children are told that a stowaway from launch day still lives in the ducts and steals socks.
People say there is a sealed deck nobody goes to, where the lights still come on at ship's night.
Locals say the first colonist planted a garden that never wilts, somewhere in the old town, and nobody can find it now.
The rumour in the bars is that the council has quietly changed the course and the destination is no longer where they say.
Every year someone hears that rations are going to be cut, and every year they aren't.
The fixer on the promenade who can mend anything and has opinions about how you broke it.
